lastContactSource: A. A. Siddiqi, Beyond Earth (NASA SP-2018-4041): launched 19:22:05 UT on 5 November 1964; battery power dropped to zero at T+8 h 43 min, so it fell silent hours after launch
destinationLabel: Solar orbit (silent within hours of launch)
name: Mariner 3
significance: Mariner 3 was the first of NASA's two 1964 Mars probes. The protective shroud over the spacecraft failed to come off during launch, so its solar panels never opened and its battery ran down within about nine hours. The extra weight also left it short of the speed it needed for Mars, and it went into an orbit around the Sun instead. Engineers traced the fault to the shroud's fiberglass layers coming apart, built an all-metal shroud, and launched its twin, Mariner 4, three weeks later.
statusNote: Launched 1964-11-05 19:22:05 UT on an Atlas-Agena D from Cape Kennedy (Siddiqi, Beyond Earth; NASA NSSDCA). The payload shroud did not separate; battery power dropped to zero at T+8 h 43 min and the solar panels apparently never deployed. It ended in a heliocentric orbit of 0.983 x 1.311 AU (Siddiqi; NASA). Path calculated (estimate, drawn dashed): no trajectory data survives, only published orbit figures. Built with tools/build_solar_orbit.py: an orbit of the published size, starting at Earth's position at launch (JPL Horizons) and propagated two-body. Its size and shape follow the published figures; its orientation is an assumption (the launch point is taken as the ascending node). The orbit's inclination isn't published, so it is drawn in the plane of Earth's orbit; only the first hours of that orbit are drawn, up to the battery failure. PATH ENDS AT LAST CONTACT (1964-11-06T04:05:00Z): after that the craft is off the map (maintainer's rule, 2026-11-27).
